extracted.intended_audience: aspiring creative writers and readers of literary/philosophical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A set of literary and artistic principles derived from Chesterton's Orthodoxy chapters on will, art, tradition, and fairy tales; aimed at guiding creation of imaginative, moral, and coherent literature (particularly fairy-tale, satire, and character-focused fiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity of will / self-limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The worship of will as a general abstract principle is self-defeating; true will is particular and every act of will is an act of self-limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton: 'Every act of will is an act of self-limitation. To desire action is to desire limitation... When you choose anything, you reject everything else.' Writing implication: portray volition as concrete, particular choices with costs; avoid praising vague 'will' or unlimited freedom. Anti-pattern: characters or authors who celebrate boundless choice without consequences (leads to paralysis or meaningless action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art through constraints (the artist loves limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is fundamentally defined by limits; the essence of a work is its frame or constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton: 'Art is limitation; the essence of every picture is the frame... The artist loves his limitations: they constitute the THING he is doing.' Writing implication: use formal, thematic, and genre constraints deliberately (shape, rules, point-of-view) to generate creativity and clarity. Example: an invented world must respect its defining limits. Anti-pattern: proclaiming absolute freedom in creation while producing incoherent or shapeless work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the internal nature of things
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot 'free' an entity from the laws of its own nature without destroying it; creative freedom must not violate the essential identity of subjects and forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton examples: 'Do not free a camel of the burden of his hump: you may be freeing him from being a camel.' For writers: maintain internal consistency of characters, species, genre conventions. Anti-pattern: altering core attributes of characters/objects mid-narrative in ways that negate their identity (breaks reader's trust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire presupposes a standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire requires an admitted standard against which to be fierce; without a moral or aesthetic standard satire becomes bodiless and ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton: 'Satire may be mad and anarchic, but it presupposes an admitted superiority in certain things over others... the curious disappearance of satire from our literature is an instance of the fierce things fading for want of any principle to be fierce about.' Writing implication: when satirizing, establish clear targets and underlying values so the satire has weight. Anti-pattern: perpetual ironic denunciation that never affirms any value—reader cannot see what is being defended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradition as extended democracy / trust common voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Tradition is democracy extended through time; trust the consensus of ordinary people and traditional narratives as sources of wisdom rather than privileging lone expert opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton: 'Tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors... Tradition is the democracy of the dead.' Writing implication: incorporate folk motifs, legends, and common-sense truths; treat collective, popular forms (folk tales, nursery tales) as valid artistic resources. Anti-pattern: dismissing folklore and popular forms as merely 'primitive' or irrelevant to sophisticated art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairy-tale logic: distinguish logical necessity from contingent facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a sharp distinction between necessities of reason (mathematical/logical) and contingent physical facts; fairy-tale imagination treats physical facts as magical contingencies rather than inevitable laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton contrasts 'the science of mental relations' (necessary truths) with 'the science of physical facts' (no intrinsic necessity). Writing implication: in fantasy or mythic writing, don't force physical events into philosophical necessity; allow enchantment and the unexpected. Anti-pattern: conflating physical repetition with metaphysical inevitability (i.e., treating historic/empirical patterns as absolute laws within a moral or imaginative frame).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'magic' language to preserve wonder and agnosticism
rubrics_metrics.description: When explaining astonishing events in fiction, prefer fairy-tale/magical language (charm, spell, enchantment) rather than pseudo-scientific 'laws' that erase mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain wonder and gratitude in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should evoke an ecstasy of adventure, a sense that life is precious and puzzling; the test of happiness is gratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton: 'It was an ecstasy because it was an adventure... The test of all happiness is gratitude.' Writing implication: aim to rekindle reader's sense of astonishment and thankfulness; portray ordinary things as miraculous. Anti-pattern: flattening experience into irony or bored detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse scientific habit with philosophic necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mistaking repeated empirical patterns for inner syntheses or necessary truths; the materialist's tendency to see 'laws' where only custom or repetition exists is a sentimental mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton: 'The ordinary scientific man is strictly a sentimentalist... because, by a dark association of his own, apple-blossoms remind him of apples.' Writing implication: in philosophically serious fiction, beware of reducing mystery to deterministic systems; keep room for plurality and surprise. Anti-pattern: giving mechanistic, totalizing explanations that erase the dramatic or moral complexity of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters and action must integrate belief and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroism and moral unity are shown when belief and practical action coexist; exemplary figures combine contemplative virtues with concrete deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton contrasts Tolstoy and Nietzsche (praise without practice) with Joan of Arc (who 'was the peasant' and 'fought'). Writing implication: create characters whose convictions lead to concrete, consequential actions; avoid abstract, purely rhetorical heroes. Example: a character who admires poverty versus one who lives and endures it—prefer the latter for moral realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective critique requires some loyalty to principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual scepticism or rejecting every doctrine undermines the ability to denounce genuine evils; to rebel effectively one must also be able to trust some things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton: 'By rebelling against everything he has lost his right to rebel against anything.' Writing implication: if a narrator or ideological stance condemns all values, the narrative loses moral force. Anti-pattern: designing a worldview of total relativism that prevents the story from taking moral or aesthetic stands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegory and fable to teach and preserve moral imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairy tales and nursery stories embed healthy moral principles (examples: 'Jack the Giant Killer' teaches opposition to pride; 'Cinderella' teaches the exaltation of the humble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton references many fairy-tale 'statutes'—e.g., 'Beauty and the Beast' teaches loving something before it is lovable. Writing implication: use allegory and mythic structure to shape moral lessons and to cultivate the reader's moral imagination. Anti-pattern: overly literal, didactic moralizing that lacks imaginative embodiment.
